story:colchis.en:
## Tragic: "Two Brothers in Ambri's Furrow" (1899)

> "I didn't kill him. I brought him home. And home would not take him."
>
> — Levy-man Giorgi, from an interrogation record

Giorgi's elder brother, Levan, worked in the mine until the mine closed. The winter passed in hunger. In spring Levan vanished, and their mother said
he had gone to sea for work. Giorgi knew perfectly well she was lying.

In the Spring of Blood, when the Grand Harness first moved, Giorgi stood in Ambri's Furrow. The rebels came out of the fog — in ragged uniforms,
with chains. In the third rank Giorgi recognised his brother's back: as children they had both fallen from a walnut tree together, and Levan had broken his shoulder blade so badly that one
shoulder still sat higher than the other.

Giorgi did not fire. He laid down his rifle and walked out into the fog, calling him by name. Levan turned, and for a moment they both stood there — two brothers, in two uniforms,
in one furrow.

Then the shooting started along the front, and Levan fell. Whose bullet it was — no one knows.

Giorgi carried his brother's body down to the village. The village elder saw the heretic's mark on his chest and said he would not be buried in this
earth. Levan was buried outside the village, by the roadside. Giorgi goes there on every leave — and tells no one why.

## Heroic: "Orovela" (1913)

> "An ox doesn't listen to an engine. An ox listens to a song. It was the same in Ambri's day."
>
> — Bego the ox-driver

Ambri's Ox — a bronze steam ox, one of the twelve — served the front for six more years after the Winter of Wire. In the autumn of
1913 its boiler went out in the middle of a gas cloud. Forty wounded lay on its bed.

Bego the ox-driver was seventy years old. He took off his gas mask so his voice would carry, stepped out in front of the ox and began to sing **orovela** — the old
ploughing song with which his grandfather had led real oxen.

The engineers say the boiler lit by itself at that moment. The ox-drivers say the ox recognised the song. Bego walked two versts through the gas, singing
and coughing, and the ox followed — slowly, along the Furrow, exactly as it had carried Ambri forty-two years before.

All forty wounded arrived alive. Bego died in the hospital three days later. Now, when Ambri's Ox moves, the ox-drivers sing orovela —
and no one says it is superstition.

story:iberia.en:
## Tragic: "The Mail Shirt" (1871–1914)

> "It always comes back. The mail shirt always comes back."
>
> — the words of a Khevsur woman

A Khevsur woman, Mzia, had one mail shirt in her house. Her father-in-law put it on on the Night of Opening, in 1871, and went to Qursha's Ravine.
The shirt came back in the autumn — a comrade brought it, folded, bloody. Mzia washed it, scrubbed off the rust and set the broken rings back in
by hand.

In 1899, in the Spring of Blood, her husband put on the shirt. He stood before the Grand Harness as the city trampled the trenches. The shirt came back in summer,
folded again.

Mzia washed it again and set the rings in again. This time the new rings were a different colour, and the shirt became two-toned.

In the spring of 1914, when the Grand Harness moved toward Ambri's grave, her grandson, sixteen-year-old Gio, put on the shirt.
Mzia walked him to the door and said nothing. Since then she watches the road every evening.

The mail shirt always comes back. Mzia knows it. She is waiting for something else.

## Heroic: "Bero's Bark" (1906)

> "For the first time in its life the dog barked at an officer. We scolded the dog. The dog was right."
>
> — notes of the Spasalari's adjutant

The Tushetian shepherd Tamar's nagazi, **Bero**, was a calm dog. In five years it had never once barked at a person — only at a devi-spawn,
and once at a bear.

In the winter of 1906 a coalition liaison officer arrived at headquarters with great ceremony: he brought new maps and the recommendation of an old engineer
from the Age of Sealing. As he went into the Spasalari's tent, Bero leapt out of the snow and blocked the door so that the officer stepped back.

Everyone said the dog had gone wild. Tamar pulled Bero away and apologised. But at night, when the officer thought everyone was asleep, Bero
barked again — this time by the storehouse where the new maps were kept. Tamar came out and saw the officer changing the line of a mountain path
on the map — exactly so that the next day's detachment would walk straight into the devis' ravine.

The Listener never made it to interrogation — he killed himself. Every map was re-checked. Since then no new person enters Iberian headquarters
until a nagazi has sniffed him — and no one finds this rule funny.

story:hell.en:
> Stories of the dark side through their own eyes: "heroism" for them is obedience; tragedy — whatever obedience cannot contain.

## Tragic: "No. 4471" (1902)

> "A recruit needs no name. A name is the enemy of order."
>
> — from the Legion's regulations

Recruit **4471** grew in a flask, like all the rest: the same face, the same voice, the same number on the arm. It was taught
the volley, the formation, the advance. Nothing more.

In the winter of 1902 the Legion took a Colchian levy-man prisoner, and 4471 was ordered to guard him. The levy-man talked all night — about his mother, his village,
his wife, whose name was **Natia**. 4471 asked what "Natia" was. The levy-man told it: a name. What they call you when they love you.

In the morning the prisoner was taken away. 4471 went to the Marquis — the first recruit in the Legion's history to speak without an order — and asked for a name.

The Marquis looked at it for a long time. Then he ordered the recruit **returned to the flask** — "due to a defect". No. 4472, which took its place, was exactly
the same. But the Legion's chronicler, as he wrote down the order, hesitated for the first time in his life — and in the margin of the record, in small letters, he wrote:
"Natia".

## Heroic: "Halphas's Seven Nights" (1908)

> "The tower was built in one night. The tower was held for seven nights. The Legion carried out its order."
>
> — the Legion's report, in full

In the Winter of Wire one file of Halphas's Garrison-Builders was given an order: in one night, build a tower in the middle of no man's land and hold it
until the Legion reached them.

They built the tower by night, in steam armour, without a sound. By morning the tower stood. The Legion did not come — the road was blocked by gas and by Iberia's Thunderbolt Gunners.

The garrison-builders held the tower for seven nights. Supplies ran out on the third day. On the fifth day their commander — a rank below Marquis — gave
an order: strip the plates from the dead's armour and hammer them into the tower wall.

On the eighth morning the Legion arrived. It found nine alive in the tower — out of forty. The Marquis wrote one sentence in his report. In the legions that is called great
praise. But the Colchian scouts who watched the tower from afar still remember: in seven nights not one sound came from the tower — no
screaming, no singing, no orders.

story:harness.en:
> The heretics come from every nation. Many of them were not brought by evil — but by hunger, anger or a promise.

## Tragic: "Bread from the Harness-Lord" (1889–1904)

> "He told us the children would have bread. The children had bread."
>
> — a rebel's last words, on the steps of the altar

Dato was a miner. When the mine closed in 1889, his three children barely made it through the winter. In spring quiet people came to the village
and said: **the Harness-Lord** needs workers underground. The wage — bread. Every week, for the family.

Dato went. The bread came — every week, for fifteen years. Dato worked at the Grand Harness's boilers, then in the trenches, then in the ranks of the rebels.
He no longer asked whom he fought for. He knew only whom he worked for.

In 1904, after Dragon's Field, when the Grand Harness fell back and had no prisoners left, the altar needed fresh blood. The lists
were filled with the names of those who had been "in debt" the longest. Dato's name was first.

He climbed the steps of the altar strangely calm. His daughter, who was working as a nurse in Colchis at the time, learned of it only ten years later
— from a wounded heretic who had known her father. "He used to say you had bread," the heretic said. The daughter dressed his wound
and made no answer.

## Heroic: "The Night of the Harness-Slaves" (1910)

> "The chain is one. If we all pull together — the chain will follow us."
>
> — the words of a captive smith

The city of the Grand Harness is hauled by prisoners in chains — two hundred, three hundred people on one chain, beside the devis. In 1910, after the Night of the Sky-Ships,
the city stood still for four months. In those four months the prisoners learned to talk to each other — in whispers, in thirteen languages.

One captive smith — an Italian named **Bruno** — checked every link of the chain by hand and found one that rust had eaten through.

When the city moved again, at night, at the edge of a ravine, Bruno gave the signal. Three hundred people at once, in one instant, pulled the chain **backward**. The rusted link
snapped. One section of the Harness — and with it two chained devis — slid into the ravine.

Half the prisoners died that same night. Half escaped into the darkness. Fifty reached the trenches of Colchis. Bruno was not among them —
he stayed by the chain to unlock the last man's shackles. After that night the Grand Harness put a double guard on every chain — and forbade the prisoners
to speak to one another.

story:listeners.en:
### Tragic: "The Gift" (1871)
**Heinrich** was a Listener for twenty years and for twenty years was proud of his work: the seal he built protected his home town, and the town raised
a monument to him. On the Night of Opening he opened his lock, like all the rest. In the morning he walked through the town — and by his monument, in the square, the first thing
he saw was what had come up out of the seal. He never went back to the Brotherhood. He stayed in the town, clearing rubble, for nine years, until someone recognised him.

### Heroic (through their own eyes): "The Empty Uniform" (1902)
The Brotherhood's sleeper **Irina** lived for five years in the Colchian levy under a false name. In 1902 her company was about to be taken by the heretics —
for the altar. The Brotherhood's order was: do not interfere. Irina led the company out at night by a marsh path that only the Brotherhood knew, and in the morning
she vanished — leaving her uniform in the trench, folded. In the Brotherhood they call her "the lost one". In the company — "our twentieth", and they leave her place in the rank empty.

story:kajeti.en:
### Tragic: "Too Good a Craft" (1890)
The kaji smith **Urma** made a captive soldier a new hand — of cast iron, with silver joints, the best she had ever made. The soldier
escaped, with the new hand, and went back to his unit. Two years later he stood at the gate of Kajeti, with the same hand, breaking down the gate. From behind the gate Urma recognised
her own work — and could not lift her hammer. Zarda took her forge away from her. The kajis say: "Don't make it so good that it works against you."

### Heroic (through their own eyes): "The Forge Under the Avalanche" (1897)
An avalanche buried the forge in the Kajeti valley, and twenty kajis and two hundred prisoners were trapped inside. The kajis did not let the forge go out: for a whole month they beat their hammers,
in one rhythm, so that the forge's heat melted a tunnel through the snow. The prisoners went out first — the kajis decided so: "the material must survive".
Half of the prisoners stayed in Kajeti of their own free will. Zarda says it was the best bargain Kajeti ever struck.

story:ring.en:
### Tragic: "The Letter No One Could Read" (1906)
**Tomasz**, a soldier of a Tithe detachment, lived for three years in a trench with a boy whose language he did not understand. They talked in signs, ate from one bowl
and guarded each other's backs. When the boy was killed, Tomasz found a letter in his pocket — to his mother. For a year he searched for an interpreter who knew that
language. At last he found one. The letter said: "There's a man here who doesn't know my language. But he is my brother." Tomasz took the letter to the mother himself —
and read it, in two languages, in the interpreter's voice.

### Heroic: "Forty Voices" (1910)
During a night attack the battalion's telephone line was cut, and forty detachments stood along the line, with forty languages. The heretics shouted false orders —
in every language the Listeners had learned. **The interpreters** walked the line on foot and had every detachment sing the same song — the battalion's
song, which everyone knows by heart, with the same tune in every language. Where the song was heard, the order was real. The false voices drowned in the song.

story:hellenic.en:
### Tragic: "The Bronze Son" (1891)
The old engineer **Stavros** assembled automaton phalanxes in the forge of Hephaestus. His son was killed on the shore of the hydras, and that winter Stavros
cast one automaton in his son's likeness — the face, the walk, the tilt of the head. The automaton fought like all the others. But every night, when the phalanx
returned to camp, it stepped out of the rank and stopped at Stavros's door — silent, until morning. The League issued an order: melt the automaton
down, the front needed the bronze. Stavros lit the furnace himself. Since then he has never given a new automaton a face.

### Heroic: "The Eye of the Storm" (1897)
When Typhon's storm neared the shore, only one of the Cyclops cannons of the Storm Wall was left whole, and of its crew — only
young **Eirini**. In the heart of the storm, they said, hides the eye of Typhon. Eirini braced the lens against the wind, waited two hours
and fired the moment the wind dropped for a single second. The storm broke apart. The cannon was found melted, Eirini — beneath it, alive. She still
assembles phalanxes — and sets a lens in each one in place of an eye.

story:northern.en:
### Tragic: "The Horn That Fell Silent" (1881)
Heimdall's hornblower **Einar** stood above the fjord, and he had his orders: do not sound until the wolves cross the bridge — so as not to raise
a false alarm. The wolves did not come over the bridge — they came over the ice, below the bridge. Einar saw them and hesitated: the order
was about the bridge. When he sounded, half the town was asleep. Since then every hornblower of the North has one rule: "When in doubt — sound."

### Heroic: "Astrid's Oath" (1902)
A new chain, woven "from impossible things", had to be wrapped around Fenrir — but the wolf would not let the chain near until someone put a hand
in its jaws, as in the old story. **Astrid** — a veteran of Tyr's One-Handed, whose one hand was already steam — stepped forward and
put in the other, living hand. The chain was bound. The wolf bit the hand off. Astrid now fights with two steam hands and says the oath is now
doubly bound.

story:celtic.en:
### Tragic: "A Friend's Eye" (1898)
There was a traitor among Lugh's Slingers, and **Rowan** found him: **Conall**, with whom he had slung stones since childhood. Rowan could have
taken him alive, but Conall stood on the shore, at the sound of a Fomorian boat, giving a signal. Rowan fired — exactly as they had learned together.
Rowan tells this story to no one — and no longer picks up a sling.

### Heroic: "Three Blows" (1913)
The bullet for Balor's eye had to be forged with three blows, without a pause — exactly as in the myth. The Fomorians attacked Goibniu's forge, and
the master smith — **Brigid** — was hit by a bullet after the first blow. She struck the second blow fallen on one knee. The third — her apprentice,
who held her hand on the hammer. The bullet is ready. In the forge it bears the marks of two hands.

story:finnish.en:
### Tragic: "The Mother of the Twilight" (1914)
**Elina's** mother was born in the first winter of the Twilight and has never seen the real sun — only Ilmarinen's steam sun, which shines but does not
warm. When the town debated putting out the steam sun, her mother told Elina: "Put it out. I lived in the twilight. You — must not." Elina carried her
voice to the assembly. On the day the decision was made, her mother died in a cold room — in the light of the steam sun.

### Heroic: "A Song for the Mountain" (1909)
Väinämöinen's Singers knew the sun was hidden in Louhi's mountain — but the mountain had no door. Thirteen singers stood at the mountain's foot and
sang for thirteen nights, with one voice, until the rock followed the song — and a crack appeared. Light came out of the crack, for just one second.
Thirteen of the singers went, nine came back. Now everyone knows where the sun is. But the thirteen nights are still needed.

story:britain.en:
### Tragic: "The Last Lesson" (1886)
The school of Beowulf's Heirs stood on the edge of the fen: forty pupils, one old teacher, one hall. One night the hall was attacked by spawn
risen from the mere — exactly as in the epic. The teacher took the children up to the loft and threw down the ladder. In the morning the only one alive
was **Wilfred**, the smallest, who had climbed to the loft last and seen everything. He now commands the fen scouts, and his detachment
never sleeps in a hall.

### Heroic: "One Lantern" (1912)
The mother's hall lies beneath the mere, and, according to the epic, one may only go down there alone. Wilfred went down in a steam diving helmet with one lantern.
The lantern went out in the third minute. He went along the wall, feeling his way by hand, until he reached the lock. The lock has not yet broken —
but Wilfred knows the way, and on the shore of the mere there is now a rope that runs all the way to the hall.
